w: What's tested Which gland makes which hormone, and the three kinds of hormones What each hormone problem looks like in the mouth and on the X-ray What to do for these patients in the chair, especially diabetics: his numbers and how to fix low sugar How to spot thyroid storm, adrenal crisis and low blood sugar His three patient cases Dr. Taylor's lecture is a review of the endocrine system for dentists. For each gland: what it makes, what goes wrong, and what you see in the mouth. Then three patients. These notes follow his recording and slides. The basics Hormones control growth, metabolism, reproduction, stress, calcium, and fluid balance. They travel in the blood, so they are slower than nerves, but they last longer and take longer to shut off. Three kinds, and he said you need to know them: amine (epinephrine, norepinephrine), peptide (insulin), steroid (estrogen, testosterone). Peptides like insulin bind on the cell surface. Steroids go inside the cell, to the nucleus. Negative feedback keeps hormones in range. When a gland's hormone gets low, the signal from the pituitary goes up. Pituitary The hypothalamus is the boss of the pituitary. The front of the pituitary makes ACTH for the adrenal cortex, TSH for the thyroid, GH for growth, FSH and LH for reproduction, and prolactin for milk. The back makes ADH, which saves water, and oxytocin. Too little ADH is diabetes insipidus: the kidneys dump water and the patient is always thirsty. That is not the sugar diabetes. Growth hormone stays all your life. Sex hormones at puberty close the growth plates, so the long bones stop growing. Wait until a young patient has stopped growing before placing an implant, or the face grows around it. Too much growth hormone before puberty makes a very tall person. After puberty it is acromegaly. Watch the jaw: it grows, the bite slides toward Class III, gaps open between the teeth, and the tongue gets big. Thyroid The thyroid makes T3 and T4, under TSH from the pituitary. They run metabolism and body heat. In thyroid surgery, the surgeon first finds the recurrent laryngeal nerve: damage it and the patient is left hoarse, usually for good. Too much (hyperthyroid): weight loss, fast heart, always hot. Teeth come in early in kids. These patients are extra sensitive to epinephrine, so go easy on the vasoconstrictor if the disease isn't controlled. Too little (hypothyroid), which you'll see far more often: tired, weight gain, slow heart. Teeth can come in late; more often you see a big tongue and slow healing. Memory trick: hyper is fast, hypo is slow. Fast heart and early teeth, or slow heart and late teeth. Thyroid storm is rare: the gland dumps a lot of hormone at once. High fever, a heart rate of 140 or more, agitated, shaky, nauseated, delirious, high blood pressure. It is life-threatening: call 911. Calcium PTH from the four parathyroids raises calcium fast. It makes bone break down (osteoclasts), makes the kidneys hold on to calcium, and has the kidneys make active vitamin D so the gut absorbs calcium. Vitamin D is the slow, long-term controller. It is activated in the kidney. Calcitonin comes from the thyroid when calcium is high. It undoes PTH. Too much PTH: bone breaks down. On the X-ray you lose the lamina dura, the thin white line of bone around each root. You can get brown tumors, which look dark (radiolucent), and the teeth get loose. Send the patient to their doctor. Too little PTH: calcium drops. Muscles twitch and lock up (tetany). Adrenal glands The outer part, the cortex, makes cortisol (stress, immune system, sugar) and aldosterone (keeps sodium, handles potassium). The inner part, the medulla, makes epinephrine and norepinephrine. That matters for the vasoconstrictor in your anesthetic and for keeping patients calm. Trick: a corticosteroid comes from the cortex. Addison disease: not enough cortisol. Low blood pressure, tired, dark skin, and brown patches in the mouth. Why brown? Low cortisol lets ACTH climb, and ACTH turns on the pigment cells. Adrenal crisis is Addison's emergency. It can be set off by a long or stressful surgery, a bad infection or injury, or a missed steroid dose. After a big procedure the patient may need extra steroid; ask their doctor how much. Look for very low blood pressure, weakness, confusion, passing out and shock. Cushing syndrome: too much cortisol, and it looks just like long-term steroid pills. Round "moon" face, a hump between the shoulders, high blood sugar. In the mouth: more infections and slow healing. Pancreas and diabetes Alpha cells make glucagon, which breaks down stored sugar and makes new sugar. Beta cells make insulin, which moves sugar into cells and stores it. Type 1: the immune system destroys the beta cells, so the patient needs insulin shots. Type 2: the body resists insulin, and insulin levels run high. The insulin is there but doesn't work. His numbers: a finger-stick under 60 means give sugar. An HbA1c above 7 means poor control, with more implant failures and more gum disease. Below 7 is good control; most people without diabetes run about 5. Metformin stops the liver from making sugar. A diabetic who took it and skipped breakfast can go low in your chair. In the mouth, diabetes brings dry mouth, thrush (candidiasis), burning mouth, slow healing, more gum disease and more cavities. Saliva comes from the blood, so high blood sugar means sugary saliva that feeds yeast and cavity germs. Gum disease and diabetes make each other worse. Keep the mouth clean. Why extractions heal slowly: high sugar, weak immune cells (neutrophils), poor blood supply and poor collagen. So expect slow healing and infection. The diabetic patient in your chair Before: check how well the sugar is controlled (HbA1c). Ask if they ate and took their medicine. Book mornings. During: watch for low sugar: sweating, shaking, confusion, a fast heart. Check a finger-stick (ask first). A glucose monitor on the arm may not read very low numbers, so check anyway. If they're awake, give straight glucose. Table sugar is half fructose, which the liver has to convert first, so glucose works faster. Drugs like Mounjaro slow the stomach, so sugar by mouth works slowly. If it fails: IV sugar, or a glucagon shot. If they pass out, activate emergency protocols. Low sugar or thyroid storm? Both shake and race. Fever and high blood pressure mean thyroid storm. Sex hormones Puberty: gums get more inflamed. Pregnancy: more estrogen and progesterone, so pregnancy gingivitis and the pyogenic granuloma, the "pregnancy tumor," a lump of gum tissue usually between two teeth. Menopause: dry mouth, changed taste, and weaker bones. His three patients Lucilla, Graves disease, heart racing, pulse 112: the thyroid is overactive, T3 and T4 are high. Go easy on epinephrine. Look for early eruption in the young, cavities, burning mouth, and a tremor that gets in the way. The danger is thyroid storm: check her heart rate first. Proximo, type 2 diabetic for 22 years, skips his metformin, glucose 220, HbA1c 9.8 percent, needs extractions, smokes a pack a day: the problem is insulin that doesn't work. Expect slow healing, check his control first, and time the visit after his meal and medicine. Pack-years are packs a day times years: a pack a day for 40 years is 40 pack-years. Commodus, Addison disease, brown patches in the mouth, blood pressure 90 over 60: the adrenal cortex is failing and cortisol is low. High ACTH causes the brown color. Long surgery, infection or a missed steroid dose can set off an adrenal crisis, and he may need extra steroid after a big procedure.
